items.title: Around 50,000 Huguenots fled to England in the 1680s
items.claim: Why did French Huguenots come to England?

options.text: They were invited as agricultural labour by William III
Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes (1598) in 1685, removing Protestant rights — around 50,000 fled to England, with major settlements in Spitalfields, Soho and Canterbury
They were exiled by James II for Jacobite sympathies
Famine in Brittany drove migration in the 1680s

items.reveal:
The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (October 1685) made Protestant worship illegal in France. Perhaps 200,000-400,000 Huguenots fled total — to England, the Dutch Republic, Brandenburg, the Cape and the American colonies.

In England they brought silk-weaving (Spitalfields), gunmaking, watchmaking, banking (the Courtauld and Bosanquet families). 'Refugee' as an English word enters the language from the Huguenot experience.

Charles II had already extended denizenship to French Protestants in 1681. Anti-Catholic sentiment made absorption relatively smooth.
items.why: Migration history in Britain is much older than the 20th century. The Huguenot case is the classic example of refugees whose skills shaped an industrial sector — and whose absorption was made easier by religious alignment.

items.title: The Luddites were skilled workers protecting trade standards

options.text: Anti-technology mystics who rejected all machinery
Skilled textile workers — stocking knitters, croppers, weavers — who smashed specific machines being used to produce low-quality goods by unapprenticed labour, often after pay cuts and food shortages

items.reveal:
The Luddites took their name from the mythical Ned Ludd. Their grievances were specific: wide stocking frames produced cut-up goods sold as stockings; gig-mills and shearing frames replaced cropping; manufacturers were ignoring the Statute of Artificers (1563) requiring seven-year apprenticeships.

The Frame-Breaking Act (1812) made machine-breaking a capital offence — Byron made his maiden speech in the Lords opposing it. 17 Luddites were hanged at York in January 1813. The historian E. P. Thompson's 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963) rehabilitated them as political actors.
items.why: 'Luddite' as an insult against anyone who dislikes new technology obscures the actual movement. They were skilled tradesmen defending wages and standards against unregulated mechanisation — not opponents of machinery in principle.

items.title: The abolition campaign invented modern political organising
items.claim: How did the 18th-century abolition movement work?

options.text: Mass petitions (1788 saw over 100 petitions with around 60,000 signatures), a sugar boycott by perhaps 300,000 households (1791-92), the Brookes ship diagram, public lectures by Clarkson, Equiano's autobiography (1789) — a prototype of modern campaigning
It relied solely on Quaker petitions
It was an underground secret movement

items.reveal:
Thomas Clarkson rode an estimated 35,000 miles gathering evidence and lecturing. Olaudah Equiano's 'Interesting Narrative' (1789) sold widely and gave testimony from a formerly enslaved African.

Josiah Wedgwood's 1787 medallion 'Am I Not a Man and a Brother?' became one of the first political logos. The diagram of the slave ship Brookes (1788) showed enslaved people packed into a hold — a mass-circulated visual that shocked public opinion.

The sugar boycott urged consumers to use East India rather than West India sugar; some sugar bowls were sold inscribed 'East India sugar not made by slaves'. Pressure on Parliament built across two decades before the 1807 Act.
items.why: The toolkit of modern protest — petitions, boycotts, visual propaganda, celebrity testimony — was assembled by the abolition campaign. Its 50-year arc to the 1833 Act is a template for sustained reform politics.
